He brought it up after he and Rogan began talking about child stars who found fame at a really young age, saying, "you get stunted in your growth" when you get famous too young.

"I mean, kudos to my dad, [be]cause he did a really good job of protecting us from that and very private," he said. "We didn't live in LA, we lived in Carmel. It was a very... as normal as it could be, in the sense that he was like, 'No, you just you need to be a normal child and learn how the world works.'"

item.title: President Trump receives big cheers from spectators during LIV Golf event at his New Jersey club
item.description: Trump received a big ovation from spectators while driving a golf cart at LIV Golf New York, held at his Trump National Golf Club Bedminster.
item.content:encoded:
LIV Golf is hosting its New York event at President Donald Trump’s National Golf Club Bedminster.

It's the third time that the upstart tour has held an event at one of the president's golf clubs.

As was the case at one previous event, President Trump himself was on hand to check things out.

TRUMP DRAWS MUCH DIFFERENT REACTION AT NBA FINALS THAN HE DID AT CFP NATIONAL TITLE GAME

According to The New York Post, the commander-in-chief received a big ovation from spectators as he drove a golf cart along the course.

It's always interesting to hear how Trump is received at various sporting events, but you can usually make a pretty good guess.

UFC fight? Huge ovation.

College football game? Big ovation.

Knicks playoff game? Boos.

So, I think it would've been kind of odd if he had been greeted with anything other than cheers at his own golf club.

Of course, the president being on hand for this weekend's event is a big deal for LIV Golf, which is going through an interesting time at the moment.

There was a time when it was a real question as to whether or not the tour would survive beyond 2026. Back in April, the Saudi Public Investment Fund (PIF) announced that it would no longer fund the tour.

TRUMP WEIGHS IN ON LIV GOLF, PGA TOUR AFTER SAUDIS PULL FUNDING OF STARTUP LEAGUE

That's a huge problem, seeing as the PIF was LIV's only funder.

However, LIV Golf CEO Scott O'Neil announced this week that the tour has an as-yet-unnamed investor lined up.

"LIV Golf has an agreement in place with a lead investor, signed by the investor and approved by the Board, to anchor the transaction and play a key role in supporting the path forward for the League’s next era, driven by and for the players," O'Neil said.

item.title: WNBA faces discipline dilemma after Carrington's 'White privilege' post targeting Indiana Fever
item.description: DiJonai Carrington posted "WHITE PRIVILEGE" on Threads after her Flagrant 2 ejection for striking Sophie Cunningham, putting the WNBA and WNBPA in a bad spot.
item.content:encoded:
Chicago Sky guard DiJonai Carrington was ejected for a Flagrant 2 foul on Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham on Saturday afternoon.

Then Carrington presumably went to the locker room and fired off a strong accusation.

A post on Carrington's Threads account shortly after her ejection read: "WHITE PRIVILEGE @indianafever."

Whoa.

WNBA COACH TORCHES LEAGUE’S OFFICIATING AFTER LATEST BIZARRE NO-CALL: ‘IT’S A F------ JOKE’

Following an ejection, a player went to the locker room and made an apparent race-based accusation. It's hard to imagine that happening in another major professional sports league without a harsh punishment from the league.

The Fever went on to beat the Sky, 90-86, but that seemed like a secondary story at best.

Carrington was tossed late in the first quarter after striking Cunningham across the head while the Fever guard attempted a layup. Officials reviewed the play and upgraded the foul to a Flagrant 2, which carries an automatic ejection. Cunningham had to be restrained following the play and appeared to show her teammates that her mouth was bleeding.

The timing of Carrington's post certainly appeared to suggest that she believed race, or "white privilege," played some role in what happened.

WNBA SUDDENLY WANTS TO STICK TO BASKETBALL AFTER YEARS OF MAKING POLITICS PART OF THE PRODUCT

While Carrington didn't specifically write, "The referees are racist," it's hard to find an alternative interpretation. Unless, since she tagged the Indiana Fever, she thinks the Fever organization is racist.

Either way, the WNBA finds itself in a terrible spot.

Either the league has to impose a harsh punishment on Carrington, which potentially angers other players in the WNBA and certain corners of the sports media, or it does nothing and risks reinforcing the perception that different racial standards apply, despite Commissioner Cathy Engelbert recently telling Congress that the league applies its rules and disciplinary processes consistently across all games and all players.

OutKick contacted the WNBA, the WNBA Players' Association and the Chicago Sky shortly after Carrington's post.

The league was asked whether it interpreted the message as an allegation that race or racial bias played a role in Carrington's ejection, whether it had spoken with Carrington about the post and whether it was reviewing the matter for potential discipline.

The Sky were similarly asked what Carrington meant, whether she was alleging racial bias in the officiating decision and whether the organization stood by her characterization.

OutKick also contacted the WNBPA, asking whether the union believes race or racial bias played a role in Carrington's ejection, whether it has evidence of racial disparities in WNBA officiating and whether it stands by Carrington's "WHITE PRIVILEGE" characterization.

None of the organizations responded prior to publication.

WNBPA SAYS IT DID NOT ASK WNBA TO DROP USA 250 ALL-STAR PATCH AFTER UNION OFFICER PUBLICLY OBJECTED

Complaints about officiating are part of professional sports. Players think they get fouled too much, coaches think opponents get favorable whistles, and fans are convinced every referee has a bet on their favorite team's opponent.

But claiming "white privilege" immediately after an officiating decision is different. It introduces the idea that officials aren't simply making good or bad basketball calls, but that race might influence how those calls are made.

If that's what Carrington meant, she should say it clearly and explain what evidence she has.

If that's not what she meant, that's pretty easy to clear up, too.

And there's another important piece of context in this specific incident.

Sophie Cunningham has become one of the WNBA's most polarizing players after publicly stating that she doesn't believe biological men should compete in women's sports. Her position has generated rallies at Fever games, subsequent counter-protests and open disagreement from others inside the WNBA, including the players' association.

So, it's entirely possible Carrington's message was aimed at something broader than the officiating.

Again, that's why clarification matters.

The WNBA can't spend years embracing players speaking publicly about politics, race, gender and social issues, then treat a player's "WHITE PRIVILEGE" accusation as something that doesn't deserve a suspension.

And the WNBPA has a problem, too. On Friday, the union said "hate, abuse, and demonization of any person or group of people, including transgender people" fuels "fear, division, and harm."

Well, if "any person or group" actually means any person or group, then the union can’t carve out an exception when one of its own players invokes "WHITE PRIVILEGE" against another team.

Carrington not only posted that accusation publicly, but she did it during a game and presumably from inside a WNBA locker room. She tagged another WNBA franchise.

The league, the players' association and the Sky were given an opportunity to explain what she meant or, at minimum, say whether they asked her.

They haven't yet.

For now, Carrington's two-word accusation is left to speak for itself.

item.title: EXCLUSIVE: Teen girls recall Jersey Shore ride malfunction that left them stuck hanging upside down
item.description: Two 13-year-olds recall the terrifying minutes they spent stuck upside down on the Wipe Out ride at Castaway Cove in Ocean City, New Jersey.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: Early last month, on the day after the Fourth of July, more than a dozen people found themselves trapped upside down on a malfunctioning ride along the boardwalk in Ocean City, New Jersey.

Charlotte Hacker and Emilia Gordon, both 13, were among the passengers on the Wipe Out ride at Playland's Castaway Cove when it got stuck that evening.

The two friends were interviewed with their parents' permission, recounting to Fox News Digital the terrifying experience of dangling midair with no idea of when they would come down.

"We were stuck upside down for five to seven minutes, and it doesn't seem like that much to the people that were down watching us, but we were up there, and it felt like an hour," Hacker said on Saturday.

EIGHT RIDERS LEFT DANGLING ATOP 100-FOOT ROLLER COASTER FOR OVER THREE HOURS AT TEXAS AMUSEMENT PARK

The girls went to the boardwalk to celebrate Gordon’s 13th birthday, which was the following day. They said they often ride the attractions there and decided to try the Wipe Out because it was new.

The ride swings like a pendulum, repeatedly turning thrill-seekers upside down while its passenger compartment spins. Only this time, the ride inexplicably stopped with everyone suspended upside down.

"I seriously thought I was going to pass out," Gordon said. "You try to put your head up, but you literally can't. You can barely get it up at all."

The girls, seated next to each other, tried to carry on mundane conversations to distract themselves while blood rushed to their heads.

SIX FLAGS GUESTS STRANDED 245 FEET IN AIR AFTER POWER OUTAGE FORCES COASTER EVACUATION

"I remember thinking that the lap bars were going to open and that we were just going to fall," Gordon said.

Family members on the ground waiting for their kids to get off the ride were terrified as well, the girls said.

"My uncle was there too, because we were all with my cousins, so he was also freaking out," Hacker said.

Eventually, the ride's operators managed to get it moving again, but to the girls' dismay, it kept on going. Once the ride finished, they said they weren't let off for another few minutes.

It is unclear what caused the apparent malfunction, and if any injuries were reported.

Hacker said the ride did not close, adding that there were some people who stayed in line and rode it after they got off.

"When we came off, people were literally clapping," Gordon said.

The amusement park offered ticket refunds to the girls, which they didn't think was sufficient after what they went through.

"That ride is five tickets, so they just gave back our ticket but [Hacker] only got three back. I got five. But still, after all that, I feel like you expect more," Gordon said.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Ocean City Fire Department, Ocean City Police Department, the ride's operator and the New Jersey Department of Community Affairs for comment.
